concepts.name: World Bank Group: Institutional Architecture and Five Constituent Bodies
key_dimensions: Distinction between 'World Bank' (IBRD + IDA) vs. 'World Bank Group' (all five institutions) — a classic UPSC trap
Year of establishment and membership eligibility differences across IBRD, IDA, IFC, MIGA, and ICSID
Which bodies require IMF membership as a prerequisite vs. which do not
Overlapping mandates and how the five bodies complement rather than duplicate each other

concepts.name: IBRD: Mandate, Membership, and Lending Modalities
key_dimensions: Original Bretton Woods mandate (post-WWII reconstruction) vs. current poverty-reduction focus
Borrower eligibility: middle-income and creditworthy low-income countries (NOT the poorest — IDA's domain)
Market-based lending rates vs. IDA concessional terms — how IBRD raises capital through bond issuance
Voting structure: weighted voting based on capital subscription vs. IMF's similar but distinct quota system

concepts.name: IDA: Concessional Financing and Replenishment Cycles
key_dimensions: Eligibility threshold: GNI per capita cutoff (IDA-eligible vs. blend countries) and periodic revision
IDA replenishment process: donor-driven triennial cycles (e.g., IDA-20, IDA-21) and their significance
Instruments: grants vs. zero/low-interest credits — conditions under which grants are provided vs. credits
India's transition from IDA borrower to IDA donor — geopolitical and developmental significance

concepts.name: IFC: Private Sector Financing Arm — Mandate and Instruments
key_dimensions: Unique feature: only World Bank Group body that lends exclusively to the PRIVATE sector without government guarantees
Instruments: equity investment, loans, guarantees, risk management products, and advisory services
IFC's role in mobilizing third-party capital — the concept of 'crowding in' private finance for SDGs
Distinction from IBRD/IDA: no sovereign guarantee required; IFC bears commercial risk

concepts.name: MIGA: Political Risk Insurance and Investment Guarantees
key_dimensions: Specific risks covered: currency transfer restrictions, expropriation, war/civil disturbance, breach of contract — NOT commercial risk
Who are the clients: investors (not governments) seeking protection for FDI into developing countries
MIGA vs. IFC overlap trap: IFC provides financing; MIGA provides guarantees/insurance — both target private sector
MIGA's role in 'de-risking' investment into fragile and conflict-affected states (FCS)

concepts.name: ICSID: Investor-State Dispute Settlement Mechanism
key_dimensions: Unique jurisdictional feature: disputes between foreign INVESTORS and sovereign STATES — not state-to-state
ICSID Convention (Washington Convention, 1965) — India's non-ratification and its implications for BIT disputes
Arbitration vs. conciliation: two distinct mechanisms available under ICSID
Controversy: sovereign right to regulate vs. investor protection — 'regulatory chill' debate relevant to India's policy

concepts.name: World Bank Voting Rights and Governance Reform
key_dimensions: Weighted voting system: basic votes + shareholding-based votes — how it differs from IMF's quota system
Voice and representation reform: shift in voting power toward developing and transition countries (2010 reform)
US veto power: US holds >15% voting share at IBRD, giving effective veto over special majority decisions (85% threshold)
Demand for greater representation by BRICS nations and the challenge to World Bank's legitimacy

concepts.name: World Bank Group and Climate Finance: Evolution of Mandate
key_dimensions: Paris Alignment commitment: World Bank pledge to align all financing with Paris Agreement goals post-2025
Climate Finance targets: proportion of lending dedicated to climate (mitigation vs. adaptation split)
Country Climate and Development Reports (CCDRs) as diagnostic tools — replacing older Country Partnership Frameworks
Criticism: continued indirect fossil fuel financing through financial intermediaries despite green commitments

concepts.name: IDA Blend Countries: The Dual Eligibility Concept
key_dimensions: Definition: countries eligible for BOTH IDA (concessional) and IBRD (market-rate) loans simultaneously
Criteria: IDA-eligible income but creditworthy enough for some IBRD borrowing (e.g., India was a blend country)
India's graduation from blend status and its implications for future borrowing terms
Policy trap: 'blend countries' should not be confused with 'graduated countries' who lose IDA eligibility entirely

concepts.name: World Bank's Safeguard Policies and Environmental/Social Framework (ESF)
key_dimensions: Shift from Operational Policies (OPs) to the new Environmental and Social Framework (ESF) effective 2018
Ten Environmental and Social Standards (ESSs) — especially ESS on indigenous peoples and involuntary resettlement
Borrower vs. World Bank responsibilities under ESF — expanded role of borrowing country
Criticism from civil society: weakening of safeguards by shifting responsibility to borrowers with weaker domestic institutions

concepts.name: World Bank Group and India: Institutional Relationship
key_dimensions: India as one of the largest IBRD borrowers historically — sector focus (infrastructure, health, urban development)
India's transition from IDA recipient to IDA donor — symbolism for South-South cooperation
IFC's investments in Indian private sector: renewable energy, financial inclusion, MSMEs
India's non-ratification of ICSID Convention and its alternative dispute resolution preferences

concepts.name: World Bank's Knowledge and Research Functions: Beyond Lending
key_dimensions: World Development Report (WDR): annual flagship publication — themes, recent editions, and policy influence
Doing Business Report: discontinued in 2021 after data irregularity scandal — implications for institutional credibility
PovcalNet / Poverty and Inequality Platform: global poverty measurement methodology ($2.15/day line)
Human Capital Index (HCI): components, country rankings, and India's performance — distinct from HDI

concepts.name: Poverty Measurement Methodology: World Bank vs. Other Frameworks
key_dimensions: International Poverty Line evolution: $1/day → $1.25 → $1.90 → $2.15 (2022 revision in 2017 PPP terms)
Difference between World Bank poverty line, UNDP's MPI (Multidimensional Poverty Index), and India's Tendulkar/Rangarajan lines
PPP (Purchasing Power Parity) adjustment rationale and its limitations for cross-country comparison
Extreme poverty vs. moderate poverty thresholds ($2.15 vs. $3.65 vs. $6.85) and their policy applications

concepts.name: World Bank Group vs. IMF: Mandate Overlap and Distinction
key_dimensions: Classic distinction: IMF = monetary/macroeconomic stability (BoP crises); World Bank = long-term development finance
Overlap area: structural adjustment conditions — World Bank's SAPs historically aligned with IMF conditionality
Joint IMF-World Bank programs: Debt Sustainability Analysis (DSA), Financial Sector Assessment Program (FSAP)
UPSC trap: both are Bretton Woods institutions but have different membership requirements, capital structures, and purposes

concepts.name: World Bank Group vs. New Development Bank (NDB) and AIIB: Competition or Complementarity
key_dimensions: NDB (BRICS Bank) and AIIB as challengers to Western-dominated Bretton Woods order — geopolitical framing
Key differences: NDB has equal voting rights for all founders; AIIB has China as dominant shareholder
World Bank's response: reform initiatives, increased infrastructure lending, and co-financing with NDB/AIIB
India's strategic positioning: founding member of both NDB and AIIB while remaining a major World Bank borrower

concepts.name: Debt Sustainability and World Bank's Role in Low-Income Country Debt Relief
key_dimensions: Joint IMF-World Bank Debt Sustainability Framework (DSF) for Low-Income Countries — traffic light risk ratings
HIPC (Heavily Indebted Poor Countries) Initiative and MDRI (Multilateral Debt Relief Initiative) — World Bank's role
G20 Common Framework for debt treatment — World Bank's advocacy role vs. IMF's coordination role
China as a bilateral creditor complicating multilateral debt relief — World Bank's limited leverage

concepts.name: World Bank's Cascade Approach and Maximizing Finance for Development (MFD)
key_dimensions: MFD principle: use private finance first; public/concessional finance only where markets fail — sequence matters
Cascade approach: private finance → public-private partnerships → public finance — policy reform as prerequisite
IFC's 'Creating Markets' strategy as operational arm of MFD agenda
Criticism: MFD may under-serve public goods (health, education) where private finance is inherently inadequate

concepts.name: World Bank's Role in Global Health and Pandemic Response
key_dimensions: Pandemic Emergency Financing Facility (PEF): launched post-Ebola, criticized for slow disbursement during COVID-19, later discontinued
Financial Intermediary Funds (FIFs): World Bank as trustee for Global Fund, GAVI, CEPI — distinction between trustee and implementing agency
COVID-19 response: IBRD/IDA fast-tracked $160 billion package — largest crisis response in World Bank history
Pandemic Fund (new, 2022): successor mechanism to PEF — governance lessons learned

concepts.name: World Bank's Evolution of Conditionality: From Structural Adjustment to Development Policy Lending
key_dimensions: Structural Adjustment Programs (SAPs) of 1980s–90s: Washington Consensus policies and criticism (austerity, privatization)
Shift to Development Policy Loans (DPLs)/Development Policy Operations (DPOs): prior actions vs. tranches
'Ownership' principle: borrower-designed programs vs. externally imposed conditions — post-SAP reform narrative
Ongoing debate: conditionality as leverage for governance reform vs. infringement on national sovereignty

concepts.name: World Bank Inspection Panel and Accountability Mechanism
key_dimensions: Inspection Panel (est. 1993): first independent accountability mechanism in any MDB — investigates harm to affected communities
Who can file complaints: directly affected people (minimum 2 persons) — NOT NGOs acting alone, NOT governments
Panel's powers: investigation and findings only — it does NOT have power to sanction or enforce remedies
Evolution to 'Accountability Mechanism' combining Inspection Panel + Dispute Resolution Service — 2020 reform
